extracted.intended_audience: general Protestant/public readers and critics judging Maria Monk's allegations (19th-century pamphlet audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and argumentation for evaluating the truthfulness of a sensational personal testimony alleging institutional crimes (here, Maria Monk's disclosures about convent abuses). Focuses on what kinds of evidence and tests make such allegations credible or not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical inspection / on-site verification
rubrics_metrics.description: The decisive test is a direct, impartial exploration of the accused premises (the Hotel Dieu Nunnery) to verify the claimant's minute descriptions of interior apartments and passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed by the New York Protestant Association: Maria offers to go to Montreal under committee protection to inspect the Nunnery; if her descriptions fail, she will submit to punishment or civil penalties. The refusal of the Priests to permit such an impartial search is treated as decisive evidence against them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity and character of those who deny the charge
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate who is denying the allegations—whether the accused parties themselves, disinterested editors, or other witnesses—as that affects the denial's weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text argues that many denials come from newspaper editors (some hostile to religion) rather than the implicated Priests; suggests denials by partisan or ignorant sources are weak compared to direct refutation by the accused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Willingness to litigate or confront in court
rubrics_metrics.description: A rightful denial should be testable by legal process (e.g., libel suit, confrontation before an impartial jury); refusal to submit to such procedures weakens the denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author challenges Priest Conroy to authorize a libel suit or to confront the authoress and publishers before an impartial jury; offers an incentive (ten dollars to a lawyer) to push the matter to legal adjudication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Competency and credibility of opposing witnesses
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess the personal character, sobriety, motives, and competence of witnesses who contradict the claimant (e.g., a mother's testimony).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mrs. Monk is characterized as habitually intemperate, of little principle, and hostile to her daughter; such facts are used to discount her sworn denial and to argue that her affidavit was likely obtained by bribery or misunderstanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent corroborative testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek corroboration from unaffiliated witnesses whose statements align with the claimant's account (e.g., teachers, neighbors, keepers of lodging).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include William Miller (who remembers Mrs. Monk saying Maria was a nun), Madame Lavalliere (who sheltered Maria and confirmed arrival in nun's habit), and other residents who attest to facts matching Maria's narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Silence or refusal of the accused as circumstantial confirmation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prolonged silence, contempt, or refusal by the accused party to allow independent investigation can be treated as circumstantial evidence supporting the claimant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues that the Priests' contemptuous posture and refusal to accept the Association's inspection proposal count strongly in favor of Maria's statements rather than against them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Physical alterations of the scene after allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Efforts by the accused or their agents to alter, conceal, or close off physical features referenced in the allegation are evidence that the original descriptions were accurate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Workmen employed by the Priests reportedly closed up subterranean passages and cells in the Hotel Dieu Convent after the allegations; such concealment is cited as corroborative proof that the passages existed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity and minute detail as evidence of firsthand knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed, characteristic, and incidental descriptions (especially those an outsider would not know) indicate that the narrator had direct experience of the places and practices described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author points to Maria's precise remarks (e.g., on how little nuns knew of the world, the making/sale of 'blessed candles') as unlikely inventions and therefore strong signs of authentic residency and observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context and timing of disclosure (death-bed / penitential motives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Confessions or disclosures made under the imminence of death or from penitential motive are treated as more credible because they remove obvious personal gain incentives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument notes that Maria's disclosures were first made when her life seemed near its end and attributes the revelations to the alarm of eternity or genuine penitence, making fabrication less plausible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voluntary risk-taking to confront accused as credibility signal
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimant's willingness to return to the locus of danger and openly confront the accused (rather than stay hidden) supports sincerity and undermines claims of fabrication or cowardly fraud.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maria's deliberate trip to Montreal, where she openly challenged Priests and offered to be confronted, is used to show she was neither deranged nor acting under compulsion, but acting from conviction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consistency with independently known public facts and practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Check whether the narrative aligns with publicly known practices, events, or phenomena (e.g., local customs, epidemics, market behavior) that an impostor would unlikely invent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites the known production and sale of 'blessed candles' in Montreal during cholera as one example where Maria's account matches public practices, strengthening her credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opponents' vagueness or lack of precise contradictory specifics
rubrics_metrics.description: When counter-evidence is vague, general, or lacking precise factual detail (dates, names, locations), its evidentiary value is reduced compared to detailed affirmative testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dr. Robertson's affidavit is criticized for not specifying with whom Maria lived or providing exact dates; such lack of detail is used to argue his testimony carries little weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Actions by third parties (officials) in response to allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete actions by other credible actors (e.g., a counsellor removing his daughter from a convent after investigating) operate as strong corroboration of the claimant's account.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A confidential counsellor, convinced by Maria's statements, returned and removed his daughter from an Ursuline Convent; his action—rather than mere words—is presented as decisive corroboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to identify named perpetrators and catalogue insiders
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimant's capacity to name and identify specific individuals associated with the alleged system indicates real acquaintance and enhances credibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maria furnished a catalogue of Jesuit priests she claimed to know; the author argues that such accurate personal identification is unlikely if her story were fabricated.
